title: Vali's question
hook: an arrow from cover, and a question the tradition still discusses
carry: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned

segments.voice: Yesterday: one arrow through seven sala trees, and Rama's word. A promise given once is kept.

Two brothers fight at a city gate. A third man, hidden behind trees with a bow, shoots one of them. And the dying brother asks a question that tellers, poets and commentators have answered in different ways. The Ramayana doesn't make this scene easy. So today, just hear it as Valmiki tells it: who does what, who says what, and in what order. Where you land afterward is up to you; the tradition has room for more than one view.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS AT THE GATE.` → `AN ARROW FROM COVER.` → `THE DYING BROTHER'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sugriva goes to Kishkindha's gate and roars a challenge. Vali comes out, and the brothers fight. Rama, watching from cover, doesn't shoot: the brothers look so alike he can't tell them apart. Sugriva is beaten and flees. So Lakshmana hangs a flowering creeper around his neck, so Rama will know him. Second challenge. This time Vali's wife Tara stops him at the door. Sugriva lost to you only today and he's back roaring, she says. He must have a powerful ally. I've heard it's Rama. Don't go. Vali goes anyway: Rama is righteous, he says, he won't do wrong. The fight begins, Vali starts to win, and Rama shoots. Dying, Vali speaks, and it's an accusation. I wasn't fighting you. You struck from hiding while I fought someone else. What wrong had I done you? Rama answers at length. This land is under the rule of Bharata's line, and I act for that rule. You took your brother's wife while he lived. And kings hunt from cover. And he says something Hindus have leaned on ever since: dharma is subtle, and hard to know. Dharma isn't a referee's rulebook. It's right action weighed in a real situation, and good people can weigh it differently. In the text, Vali accepts the answer. Some readers find it enough; others, including commentators and poets, find the scene troubling, and some later tellings change it. Valmiki keeps both the question and the answer. That's the teaching: in this tradition, even Rama's choices can be honestly questioned.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS TOO ALIKE TO TELL.` · `TARA'S WARNING.` · `VALI'S QUESTION, RAMA'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit with a question that doesn't resolve easily, from today's story or from your own life. Breathe in and let it be there; breathe out and don't answer it yet. If you pray, offer the question itself, not a verdict. Each time you start arguing with yourself, come back to the breath.
Vali. King of Kishkindha, Sugriva's elder brother, shot by Rama's arrow today, who asks why and hears Rama's answer.
Your line: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned. Valmiki kept Vali's question in. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vali's death is discussed at length in Ramayana commentary; traditional commentators defend Rama's action in several ways, while some later tellings and modern readers question it.

Vali.meaning: king of Kishkindha, Sugriva's elder brother

Kishkindha.meaning: the monkey kingdom, ruled by Vali

Bharata.meaning: Rama's brother, who rules while Rama is in exile

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, beside him in exile

dharma.meaning: right action, duty, the way things should be
